*Reasoning in voice:*

Well, I've been at this 50 years on the same ground, so I don't need to think too hard about most of it. Six and a half mu isn't much — my son takes the bulk of what the old family land ever was — but it's enough to keep me busy and put grain in the bin. With just myself in the house now, I can't do the heavy work like I used to. I pay the machinery brigade for planting and combining both crops. My back won't carry fertilizer bags across the field the way it did twenty years ago.

For the wheat going in this October — I planted Jimai 22 last year and it did fine, about 470 kg/mu, so I'll stick with it. I know some of the younger fellows are trying Shannong 28 but at my age I don't chase new varieties unless I have reason to. I'll put down compound fertilizer (15-15-15) before rotary tillage, about 50 kg/mu, and topdress 15 kg of urea at jointing if the stand looks pale. That gives me roughly 17 kg N, 7-8 kg P, 7-8 kg K per mu — plenty for a 450-500 kg yield on this soil. I've been doing split N for years; extension told me back in the nineties it was better and my own eyes confirmed it.

Irrigation: I'll water once before winter (thawing water is important for a good stand here), once at jointing, and once more at grain filling if May is dry. Three waterings is usually what the wheat needs. The well electricity is metered and it adds up, but skipping the jointing water costs more in yield than it saves.

Herbicide in early spring for the bindweed and broadleaf — I use the tractor sprayer, hire the neighbor's boy for half a day. One insecticide pass for aphids at flowering if I see them, not every year.

For maize — it goes in the ground within three or four days of wheat harvest in mid-June. That turnaround is brutal and the only way I manage is the custom planter comes through. I plant Zhengdan 958 or something similar, a mid-maturity hybrid. Compound fertilizer at planting (about 40 kg/mu of 15-15-15) and one urea topdress at the big-bell stage (V10 or so), 15 kg/mu. Maize doesn't need as much pre-plant fertilizer as wheat because it grows in warm weather and takes up nutrients fast.

Maize irrigation depends on summer rain. Most years the July-August rains carry it and I irrigate once at tasseling if dry. Last few years summer rain has been less reliable though, so I budget for two waterings.

Pesticide: herbicide at the 3-4 leaf stage, and I watch for fall armyworm now — didn't exist when I started but the last few years it's become something to look out for.

I'm cash fine, not rich, but I have savings and a small pension. I'd rather spend a bit extra on fertilizer and get the yield than cut corners. At my age the grain is partly food security — I eat from the wheat, sell the maize.
